description: We are interested in AI/ML and are really excited to apply it to NASA data in an advanced project. In our free time, we enjoy building video games and coding applications to help our community!
summary:
The Athena lander landed 250m away from its target site in a crater where the sun never reached higher than just a few degrees above the horizon. It died after just 13 hours. Lander missions on the south pole of the moon experience the sun skimming along the horizon. Only one 'hill' will determine if your lander has solar power and the ability to communicate.

Earthset is a free web application which tells you instantly if your site will be illuminated on any given day. This application uses real horizon data calculated from NASA LRO laser altimeter data. The sun and earth are placed accurately onto the landscape using NASA/JPL ephemeris data. The accuracy of positioning matches NASA/JPL Horizons to 0.00003° and can be instantly verified by anyone with one click.

You can ask Earthset any question in plain English or select up to 4 sites to get an instant GO/NO GO. If the launch window slips you can find a new date, site or better illuminated area. You can plan drives for rovers to ensure they stay illuminated. You can also rank potential sites for a lunar base to have the best solar, communication and nearby ice.

Athena showed that just a few hundred metres can decide a mission, and with Earthset anyone can check those few hundred metres before launch.
details:
Earthset answers the first questions for your lunar mission: will there be enough sunlight for the lander, and will there be a direct communications link with Earth? And if there is a delay, what will happen? At the south pole of the Moon, the Sun never rises above 2 degrees, so it just circles around the sky. This means every hill and crater rim casts a shadow several km long. Areas change from being in sunlight to being in darkness from day to day. Two points on the Shackleton ridge, only 80m apart, get 64% and 86% sunlight over 16 years. Earthset provides a clear view of this to help you make a decision in seconds, simply by using a web browser.

Type in a question in simple English, and Earthset will create a scenario showing you the sites, date, length of mission and delay. There is also an option to use the Google Gemini assistant to interpret looser questions. It will provide a short summary, but it only uses figures calculated by Earthset. You can select up to 4 sites. Each site gives you a clear GO or NO-GO with the reasoning provided in simple English, for example "Lands in the dark" or "Earth drops out of view for up to 36 hours at a time". This is based on rules you can alter: the minimum sunlight, the maximum darkness the lander can survive and the minimum communications with Earth.

The planner has clear sections. The sky section shows you a realistic 360 degree view of the horizon and where the Sun and Earth will be during the mission. Pressing play shows you the Sun going behind a hill. The timeline tells you how much sunlight there is and when Earth is visible for each site, hour by hour. It also tells you which NASA Deep Space Network dish will be able to receive from the Moon (California, Spain or Australia). The landing calendar gives a score to each landing day for the next 2 years, which shows you how a delay will affect your landing. The ranking feature tells you which of the 19 pre-set sites is the most flexible with delays. The rescue feature recommends the next best date, other sites on the same date and areas with more sunlight a few hundred metres away. Earthset also shows real shadows on the area surrounding the site. These can be viewed in real time during the mission or as an average over the entire mission, on a flat map or a 3D topographical map. There is also a battery model showing whether the lander will survive based on the real sunlight.

There are also extra features. Follow the light helps you plan a drive for your rover so that it stays in sunlight. It calculates the shadows every 6 hours of the mission. It then searches for the best drive available for your rover at the speed you choose, whilst avoiding slopes greater than 20 degrees. At Malapert Massif, driving 579m during a 14 day mission starting on 15 January 2027 increases sunlight from 85% to 100% and removes a night of 2 days and 6 hours. The Base camp finder helps you decide where to put a long-term base. It calculates how often sunlight and Earth are visible over an entire year for each 120m patch of ground. It also highlights areas that were in complete darkness all year, where water ice can survive. It then ranks the best areas for your base. The best area near the Shackleton ridge is 424m north of the landing point. The Sun and Earth are both visible there for 51% of the year, compared to 38% at the landing point, and it is only 1.4km from completely dark ground.

Earthset is also made for the public. The homepage shows you a live view of the sky over a ridge at the south pole, and you can watch the next 30 days as a time lapse with captions. The "Can the Moon see you?" feature tells you whether you and a lander on the ridge are in view of each other right now, and when you will next be in view. You can check this for 13 cities around the world or for your own location. There is also a free teachers page with 3 printable activities for grades 6-12, linked to NGSS standards. You can share any scenario as a link, save it as a mission card, export it as a calendar showing the nights of your mission, export it as a CSV file, or print it as a 1 page summary.

Behind the scenes, Earthset uses NASA/JPL's DE440 planetary ephemeris and lunar orientation kernels (SPICE) to calculate where the Sun and Earth are, taking into account light time and aberration. We compressed this data into small polynomial tables with less than 0.02 arcseconds of error, which means the calculations can be done in the browser for the years 2024-2039 with no server. For each site, we traced the horizon using NASA LRO LOLA laser altimeter data at resolutions from 20m to 474m per pixel. We traced 720 directions out to 450km, taking into account the curvature of the Moon, from 2m above the surface. The Sun is treated as a disc 0.53 degrees wide, and we calculate how much of it is visible above the landscape. Earth is treated as visible if its centre is above the horizon. We also take eclipses into account. Once we have calculated the results for each hour, we score them against your mission rules to produce the verdicts, calendar, ranking and rescue options. Custom sites, shadow maps, rover routes and base camp searches are all calculated in real time in a background thread. The rover routes are calculated using dynamic programming, which finds the sunniest route to each point at the rover's speed and then traces back to find the best route.

We have thoroughly tested Earthset. We compared 26,936 Sun and Earth positions at 7 sites from 2025 to 2038 with NASA/JPL Horizons, NASA's reference tool. The largest difference was 0.00003 degrees, which is about 1/10,000 of the width of the Sun. There is also a "Check it live against NASA" button, which repeats the comparison for the current minute. During testing, the two matched to within 0.1 arcseconds. We also tested Earthset against real missions. For JAXA's SLIM in January 2024, Earthset shows that the Sun was in the east at landing, which explains why the west-facing panels did not produce any power. It also shows that sunset came on 31 January, the day SLIM lost power to the lunar night. For Intuitive Machines' IM-2 Athena in March 2025, the Sun never rose above 5.4 degrees at its target. For IM-1 Odysseus in February 2024, there was sunlight until 2 March, but because the lander was tilted, it could not use it. For Firefly's Blue Ghost in March 2025, Earthset shows the eclipse ending at 08:34 UTC, and the lander photographed the end of the eclipse at around 08:30. We have an automated testing suite of 35 tests, which check the ephemeris, horizons, eclipses, shadows, site behaviour, battery model, rover routes and base camp finder. We also tested our polar topography against NASA's independent global topography grid and found no bias and an RMS difference of 14-20m.

Several recent landers have lost power or ended early due to the lighting and orientation at the landing site. Earthset makes this quick and easy to see before launch. You can quickly compare sites and dates if your schedule changes, test your rover routes against the moving shadows, and find good locations for your base. As NASA's VIPER team said, "Shadows move around the South Pole of the Moon at about the same speed the rover drives." The same tool can be used by students, teachers and the public to understand why the lunar south pole is so challenging. Earthset is free to use, requires no login, and its core calculations can be done offline.

Whilst there are existing maps of the polar regions of the Moon, Earthset takes this information and makes it actionable. You can type in a question in simple English, see how a delay affects every site, get a rescue plan, plan a rover route that outruns the shadows, rank the best Moon base sites based on power, communications and ice, and verify the maths against NASA. You can also see Earthset's predictions for real missions next to what actually happened.

We took many things into consideration when designing Earthset. Accuracy was key: all figures come from NASA data and have been verified against NASA/JPL Horizons. We designed Earthset for 2 different audiences. Mission planners can see the figures, whilst students and the public can read simple language. Each panel has a short guide explaining what you are seeing, how to read it and what to try. We made it accessible from the start. Text can be made larger, colours can be switched to high contrast, and the charts can use colours that work for colour-blind people. Users can also reduce movement, switch to easier-to-read spacing, and have answers read out loud. All charts have screen reader descriptions, the tabs can be navigated using the keyboard, and there are skip links. We made it fast and free to use, with no installation or accounts needed. We also made it private: there is no tracking, and a visitor's location is only used in their own browser, and only if they choose to share it. We used AI only where it helps. Gemini reads questions and writes short summaries, but figures are never created by AI, and Earthset can be used fully without it.

We are also transparent about our limitations. Custom sites, rover routes and base camp searches use lower resolution topography, so they are for screening purposes only. Ground that is dark all year indicates possible ice, but it does not confirm it. GO/NO-GO only takes into account sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth; it does not cover thermal constraints, surface hazards or relay satellites. For the Blue Ghost site, our sunset prediction differs by about 2 hours from what Firefly reported. This is due to the coarser topography grid used at that latitude and amounts to about 1 degree of Sun elevation.

Earthset was built using JavaScript, HTML and CSS. We used Canvas for the charts and maps, WebGL for the 3D topography, Web Workers for the intensive calculations, and the Web Speech API for reading answers aloud. The data was prepared and validated using Python (NumPy, spiceypy for NASA's SPICE toolkit, and Pillow), Node.js scripts and the NASA/JPL Horizons API. The site is hosted on Vercel, with 2 small functions running on the server: one passes questions to the optional Google Gemini assistant, and the other asks NASA/JPL Horizons for the live verification. We tested Earthset using an automated testing suite in Node.js and headless Chrome at desktop and phone sizes. No hardware was used.

The Moon is about to get busy. More landers are heading for the south pole in the next few years, and NASA plans to send astronauts there through Artemis. Every one of those missions will face the same two questions: will there be light, and can we call home? Athena showed that a few hundred metres can decide the answer. Earthset puts that answer in anyone's hands, whether they are a mission planner, a student or someone looking up at the Moon from their backyard, using NASA's own data and checked against NASA's own system. We built it so that the next lander doesn't have to find out the hard way.
